:knowledge-point/_canonical-example.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2^x +1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	&= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \[5pt]
			        			&=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot  \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{e^{3x}  \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2}
		}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=(3x+5)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=6x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=6(3x+5).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6x){(3x+5)}^{2}-(3{x}^{2})\cdot 6(3x+5)}{{((3x+5)^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6x(3x+5)(3x+5-3x)}{{(3x+5)}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6x(3x+5)(5)}{{(3x+5)}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{30x}{{(3x+5)}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)$ and the denominator $v(x)=4x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=7{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2),\,{v}^{′}(x)=4.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(7{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2))(4x)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)(4)}{(4x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2))}{16{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{⧸}4(7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2))}{\text{⧸}4(4{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{7x{sec}^{2}⁡(7x-2)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x-2)}{4{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{ln}({x}^{3})$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{3}+2.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{'}(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,{v}^{'}(x)=3{x}^{2}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{x})({x}^{3}+2)-(\operatorname{ln}({x}^{3}))(3{x}^{2})}{({x}^{3}+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{3}+2)-3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{3})}{x({x}^{3}+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}-3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{3})+6}{x({x}^{3}+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider a function $g(x)$ such that $g(2)=-2$ and ${g}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{2}.$ If $h(x)=\frac{5-25f(x)}{g(x)+3},$ then ${h}^{′}(2)=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        .
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
In part 2 we found that ${f}^{′}(2)=-\frac{21}{25}.$ Also,

$$
f(2)=\frac{7}{2\cdot {2}^{2}-5\cdot 2-3}=-\frac{7}{5}.
$$

The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=5-25f(x)$ and $v=g(x)+3.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-25{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-25{f}^{′}(x)\cdot (g(x)+3)-(5-25f(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x)+3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=2,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & =\frac{-25{f}^{′}(2)\cdot (g(2)+3)-(5-25f(2))\cdot {g}^{′}(2)}{(g(2)+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-25\cdot (-\frac{21}{25})\cdot (-2+3)-(5-25\cdot (-\frac{7}{5}))\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{(-2+3)^{2}} \\  & =21-20 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=(x+1)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{2}+1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2(x+1),\,{v}^{′}(x)=2x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2(x+1))({x}^{2}+1)-((x+1)^{2})(2x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)-2x(x+1)^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(({x}^{2}+1)-x(x+1))}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{2}-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(1-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-{x}^{2})}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}},\,{v}^{′}(x)=2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}})(2x)-(\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})(2)}{(2x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}-2\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4{x}^{2}\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=(x+1)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x+3.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2(x+1),\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)\cdot (x+3)-(x+1)^{2}\cdot 1}{(x+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)[2(x+3)-(x+1)]}{{(x+3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)[2x+6-x-1]}{{(x+3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x+5)}{{(x+3)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the denominator $v(x)={e}^{2x}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x})({e}^{2x})-(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{e}^{2x}}{x}-2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{e}^{2x}-2x{e}^{2x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(1-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(x)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(1)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})sin\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})-cos\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})}{{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})(-1)-0}{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)={e}^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x+2.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3{e}^{3x})(x+2)-{e}^{3x}(1)}{(x+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3x+6-1)\,{e}^{3x}}{(x+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3x+5)\,{e}^{3x}}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of ${y}^{′}(x)$ at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =\frac{(3(1)+5)({e}^{3(1)})}{((1)+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8{e}^{3}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)={e}^{3{x}^{2}}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x-2.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=6x{e}^{3{x}^{2}},\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6x{e}^{3{x}^{2}})(x-2)-({e}^{3{x}^{2}})(1)}{(x-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3{x}^{2}}(6x(x-2)-1)}{(x-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6{x}^{2}-12x-1){e}^{3{x}^{2}}}{(x-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
